study_identification.title: Mapping the Heterogeneous Brain Structural Phenotype of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using the Normative Model

study_characteristics.study_objective: To combine non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and normative modeling to individually parameterize neurobiological heterogeneity in participants with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The study aimed to identify homogeneous subgroups with distinct neuroanatomical deviation patterns and clinical phenotypes.

dataset_name.answer: ABIDE II (for training normative model); ABIDE I (for validation and clinical application)

hc_n.answer: 564 (ABIDE II for normative model training); 560 (ABIDE I for validation)

hc_age.answer: ABIDE II TD: mean 15.12 years; SD 9.45; min 5.80; max 64.00. ABIDE I TD: mean 17.22 years; SD 7.75; min 6.50; max 56.20

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: CAT12 (Computational Anatomy Toolbox 12); SPM; voxel-based morphometry; isotropic Gaussian smoothing kernel (FWHM = 10 mm)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Visual inspection for motion artifacts by three experienced personnel. Image quality divided into five levels with scores 1-5 (5 indicating best quality, 1 indicating poor quality). Participants with average score less than 3 were excluded. Quality control resulted in final sample of ABIDE II TD (n=564), ABIDE I TD (n=560), and ABIDE I ASD (n=496).

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Site effects were handled as covariates in the generalized linear model (GLM) used to regress out confounds. The GLM was used to regress out effects of age, gender, handedness, Full Scale IQ, and sites from the weights before conducting group comparisons and deviation analyses. For group analysis, 515 TD and 452 ASD participants were included after excluding subjects with missing phenotypic data (handedness and FSIQ).

modeling_method.answer: GPR (Gaussian Process Regression) with NMF (Non-negative Matrix Factorization) for dimensionality reduction

software_tool.answer: GPy (https://github.com/SheffieldML/GPy) for GPR; l0-sparse-NMF (https://github.com/smatmo/l0-sparse-NMF) for NMF; MATLAB R2015b; scikit-learn for Gaussian mixture clustering

response_variable.answer: Weights of six NMF factors derived from gray matter volume (GMV). Each factor represents a spatial pattern of gray matter distribution: Factor 1 (medial cortex including cingulate and medial frontal gyrus), Factor 2 (cerebellum), Factor 3 (occipital lobe, inferior parietal lobule, thalamus), Factor 4 (parietal lobe), Factor 5 (frontal lobe), Factor 6 (limbic system)

predictor_effects.answer: Age and gender were used as covariates (fixed effects) in the Gaussian process regression model to predict the expected weights of factors

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses some aspects of nuisance structure but not comprehensively. Age, gender, handedness, Full Scale IQ (FSIQ), and site effects were regressed out using a generalized linear model (GLM) before comparing weights and deviations between groups. However, the normative model itself only included age and gender as predictors, not site as a group-level effect or other potential sources of variance heterogeneity. The study did perform 10-fold cross-validation to assess generalizability, but there was no explicit evaluation of whether the model adequately captures heteroscedasticity, non-linear age effects beyond what GPR naturally handles, or other forms of nuisance structure.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To exclude the effects of covariates on weights, we used the generalized linear model method to regress out age, gender, handedness, FSIQ, and sites when comparing the difference of weights and deviations between ASD and TD. (Supplement, page describing 'The relative contribution of FSIQ on the weights'). For the weight of ABIDE II TD, the normative models were estimated. In each model, the weight of factor was the response variable, and age and gender were covariates. (Main text describing normative modeling)
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Supplement page describing FSIQ effects; Main text Methods section on Normative Modeling (lines 49-52)

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study used 10-fold cross-validation on the ABIDE II TD dataset to assess the generalizability of the normative model before applying it to the discovery cohort (ABIDE I). This is a validation using non-independent subsets of the same training dataset.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: To assess the generalizability of the model, we used 10-fold cross-validation before applying the model trained on ABIDE II TD to a discovery cohort. We partitioned the data into 10 'folds' and repeatedly trained the model on 90% of the data, withholding the remaining 10% for estimating generalization performance. This procedure was repeated 10 times so that each 'fold' was excluded once.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study does not perform validation on an independent held-out sample from the same domain (ABIDE II). The 10-fold cross-validation uses non-independent subsets of the training data, and the ABIDE I dataset is considered a different domain (different collection, different participants). There is no mention of setting aside an independent test set from ABIDE II TD before training.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: No explicit statement or procedure describing an independent validation set from ABIDE II TD. The paper proceeds directly from cross-validation to application on ABIDE I.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The normative model was trained on ABIDE II TD participants and then applied to ABIDE I TD and ABIDE I ASD participants, which represents validation on a different domain (different data collection, different cohort). Additionally, a reproducibility analysis was conducted where the process was reversed: NMF was performed on ABIDE I TD, normative models were trained on ABIDE I TD, and then applied to ABIDE II TD and ABIDE II ASD.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: NMF was first applied on the ABIDE II TD GM matrix, which was decomposed into six latent factors and corresponding weights. Then, the NMF back-reconstruction algorithm was used to reconstruct the ABIDE I ASD and ABIDE I TD GM matrices... we developed a normative model by training a GPR on the ABIDE II TD cohort. (Main text, Methods). Reproducibility analysis: We added four steps to examine the robustness and generalizability of our work. First, to estimate the generalizability of the NMF algorithm, we implemented NMF on the GM matrix of ABIDE I TD and obtained six latent factors and corresponding weights... To establish the robustness and generalizability of the normative model, weights of the six latent factors derived from ABIDE I TD were used to generate normative models, and deviation of the six weights relative to the norm range were computed and compared between ABIDE II TD and ABIDE II ASD.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Main text Methods lines 48-52; Supplement Reproducibility analysis section (lines 174-180)

clinical_groups_n.answer: ASD: 496 (after quality control); ASD: 452 (after excluding subjects with missing phenotypic data); ASD: 272 (with complete ADOS scores for subtyping analysis)

clinical_groups_age.answer: ABIDE I ASD: mean 17.37 years; SD 8.52; min 7.00; max 64.00. For group analysis (n=452): mean 16.85 years; SD 7.90; min 7.00; max 58.00. For subtyping (n=272): Subtype 1: mean 17.05 (SD 8.78) [7.13-55.4]; Subtype 2: mean 17.51 (SD 6.79) [7.15-38.76]; Subtype 3: mean 17.13 (SD 8.19) [8.2-39.2]

deviation_metric.answer: W-score: factor-specific deviation score calculated as (Weight_NMF_reconstruction - Weight_predict) / sqrt(variance), where Weight_predict and variance are estimated from the Gaussian process regression. The W-score quantifies how much an individual participant differs from the reference cohort in each factor. Covariates (age, gender, handedness, FSIQ, sites) were regressed out using GLM.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Two-sample t-tests were used to examine group differences in weights and deviations between ABIDE I ASD and ABIDE I TD (FDR correction applied). Pearson correlation analysis was performed between residual weights in factors and ADOS scores (communication, social, RRB) with Bonferroni correction (p<0.05/18). Gaussian mixture clustering was used to identify ASD subtypes based on deviation matrix. One-way ANOVA and chi-square tests were used to compare demographic and clinical characteristics across subtypes. Post-hoc comparisons between subtypes used two-sample t-tests with FDR correction.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Individuals with ASD showed heterogeneous deviation patterns from the normative model across six brain structural factors, and could be clustered into three distinct neuroanatomical subtypes with different clinical symptom profiles in social communication deficits.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Six latent factors were identified through NMF of gray matter volume, representing distinct brain regions with different functional profiles (affect, motor control, perception, action, cognition, memory). Compared to TD, ASD participants exhibited significantly increased weights in factors 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 (p<0.05, FDR corrected). Weights in factors 1 and 4 correlated with ADOS communication scores (r=0.185, p=0.002; r=0.181, p=0.0028, Bonferroni corrected), while weights in factors 2, 4, 5, and 6 correlated with ADOS social scores (r=0.210-0.217, p<0.001, Bonferroni corrected). ASD participants showed significantly increased deviations from the normative model in factors 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 compared to TD (p<0.05, FDR corrected). Three ASD subtypes were identified: Subtype 1 (n=143, all positive deviations ranging 0-0.5), Subtype 2 (n=76, all negative deviations), and Subtype 3 (n=53, all positive deviations >0.5). Significant differences in ADOS communication scores were found between subtypes 1 and 2 (p_FDR=0.003) and between subtypes 2 and 3 (p_FDR=0.020). Significant differences in ADOS social scores were found between subtypes 1 and 2 (p_FDR=0.013) and between subtypes 2 and 3 (p_FDR=0.008). No significant differences were found across subtypes in ADOS RRB scores. Reproducibility analysis using ABIDE I for training and ABIDE II for validation showed similar patterns, with Dice coefficient of 0.530 for clustering stability.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: First, only age and gender were considered as independent variables in the normative model; cognitive scores and home environment were not included. Second, despite demonstrating stability and robustness of clustering, the study did not find brain-symptom correlations within or across subtypes, potentially due to complex non-linear relationships between brain imaging and symptom dimensions. Third, the analysis was limited to structural MRI; other modalities including resting-state fMRI, diffusion tensor imaging, and genetic data need to be incorporated. Fourth, no factors were found to be associated with ADOS RRB scores, suggesting the method may not capture fine-grained circuitry related to repetitive behaviors. Fifth, the study is cross-sectional and cannot address developmental trajectories.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The data-driven framework combining NMF and normative modeling provides a strategy for delineating heterogeneity in ASD that can be generalized to other mental disorders with high levels of heterogeneity, such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. The approach demonstrates that individuals with ASD have heterogeneous deviation patterns in brain structure rather than a single consistent pattern, supporting the need to test for subtypes in neuroimaging studies. The stratification of ASD into biologically homogeneous subgroups may guide prognostic and precision medicine approaches. The method provides individualized, quantitative metrics that complement conventional group-level analyses. Future work should investigate effective interventions suited for different subtypes and incorporate longitudinal designs to parse heterogeneity within a developmental framework.

general_notes.general_notes: This study is innovative in combining dimensionality reduction (NMF) with normative modeling to create individualized, interpretable metrics of brain structural deviation in ASD. The NMF decomposition into 6 factors provides more interpretability than high-dimensional voxel-wise analyses. The optimal number of factors (K=6) and sparsity parameter (lambda=0.3) were determined through reconstruction error analysis and reproducibility testing between ABIDE I and ABIDE II. The NMF procedure was repeated 100 times to reduce the influence of random initialization. Meta-analytic decoding using NeuroSynth was used to characterize the functional profiles of each factor, providing neurobiologically meaningful interpretations. The back-reconstruction algorithm of NMF was used to ensure that factors from the training cohort (ABIDE II) could be applied to new cohorts (ABIDE I), which is a key strength for generalizability. The study includes extensive reproducibility analyses by reversing the training/validation datasets (ABIDE I for training, ABIDE II for validation), which showed similar patterns of results. The relationship between age and weights, and between gender and weights, was thoroughly examined in supplementary analyses. The study also demonstrated that weights can predict age using random forest regression (r=0.582 within ABIDE II; r=0.453 from ABIDE II to ABIDE I), supporting the validity of the derived features. The full list of participant IDs is provided in the supplement. ABIDE II sites are described as independent from ABIDE I sites or representing newly collected data from independent participants at overlapping sites. The proportion of females in Subtype 2 was higher than in the other two subtypes (p=0.036, chi-square test), suggesting potential sex differences in neuroanatomical deviation patterns. The Calinski-Harabasz score and Silhouette score were used to determine the optimal number of clusters (K=3). Software packages used include: CAT12 for VBM, NeuroSynth for meta-analytic decoding, MATLAB R2015b for statistical analysis, l0-sparse-NMF for matrix factorization, GPy for Gaussian process regression, and scikit-learn for Gaussian mixture clustering.
